n: Pyrexia of Unknown Origin in Children

faq.a: At least 14 days of temperature ≥38.3 °C on several occasions.
faq.q: What is the minimum duration of fever to call it PUO?

faq.a: High endemicity, seasonal transmission, and limited access to prompt treatment.
faq.q: Why is malaria still a top cause in East Africa?

faq.a: When clinical scoring, chest X‑ray, and TB‑specific labs strongly suggest TB and the child is deteriorating.
faq.q: When should I start anti‑TB therapy without a confirmed culture?

exam: What initial investigations would you order for a 5‑year‑old with 3 weeks of fever and weight loss in a rural hospital? — Full blood count, ESR/CRP, malaria RDT, urine microscopy, blood cultures, chest X‑ray; prioritize malaria RDT and blood count.

A child has PUO, hepatosplenomegaly, and a positive malaria smear with low parasitaemia. How do you interpret this? — Treat malaria but continue work‑up for co‑infection (TB, HIV) because low parasitaemia may be incidental.

How does the presentation of TB differ from bacterial sepsis in PUO? — TB shows insidious onset, night sweats, weight loss, high ESR; sepsis presents with acute high‑grade fever, tachycardia, hypotension.

Why is ceftriaxone preferred over aminoglycosides as empiric therapy in this setting? — Ceftriaxone covers common Gram‑negative and Gram‑positive organisms and is less nephrotoxic; aminoglycosides need renal monitoring.
What red‑flag sign would make you admit a child with PUO to a high‑dependency unit? — Persistent fever >40 °C with altered mental status or shock signs.
How would you manage PUO if blood cultures are unavailable? — Start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics based on local resistance patterns, treat malaria if endemic, and monitor response closely.

Explain why drug fever should be considered after 7 days of new medication. — Fever persists despite negative infection work‑up and resolves after stopping the drug, indicating a hypersensitivity reaction.
What distinguishes Kawasaki disease from other causes of PUO in a toddler? — Presence of conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes, extremity edema, and coronary artery risk; fever ≥5 days.
ai.title: Pyrexia of Unknown Origin in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Persistent fever >38.3 °C for ≥14 days without an obvious source. In low‑resource settings, a stepwise approach prioritises common tropical infections and pragmatic investigations.

b: Rule out obvious sources (e.g., obvious infection, trauma).
Document fever pattern, associated symptoms, travel, exposures.
sections.p: PUO is defined as a temperature ≥38.3 °C on several occasions lasting at least 14 days, with no diagnosis after an initial focused history, exam and basic labs.

b: Stable: well‑appearing, normal vitals except fever.
Unstable: tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status, respiratory distress.
sections.p: Severity is judged by clinical stability and organ dysfunction rather than a formal stage system.

b: Infections: malaria, tuberculosis, HIV‑related opportunists, typhoid, bacterial sepsis, brucellosis, schistosomiasis.
Inflammatory: systemic lupus erythematosus, Kawasaki disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
Malignancy: leukemia, lymphoma.
Miscellaneous: drug fever, herbal toxin exposure, prolonged fever after vaccination.
sections.p: Group causes into infections, inflammatory/autoimmune, malignancy, and miscellaneous. In East Africa, infections dominate.

b: Weight loss >5 % in 1 month suggests chronic infection or malignancy.
Hepatosplenomegaly points to malaria, TB, leishmaniasis, lymphoma.
sections.p: Child often appears ill but may be relatively well‑looking; fever may be intermittent or continuous. Look for weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, joint swelling.
Start with inexpensive, widely available tests; expand based on findings.

t.b: Is there anemia, leukocytosis, or atypical cells? Anemia with high ESR suggests chronic infection; blasts raise suspicion of leukemia.
Detect bacteremia or fungal sepsis. If unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical picture.
Positive indicates malaria; repeat if fever persists after treatment.
Identify urinary tract infection; pyuria with sterile culture may suggest TB urinary involvement.
Look for TB, pneumonia, mediastinal mass. If X‑ray unavailable, clinical TB scoring can be used.
Positive guides work‑up for opportunistic infections; if unavailable, consider clinical risk factors.

t.a: Tuberculin skin test or GeneXpert (if sputum obtainable)
t.b: Positive supports TB; GeneXpert also detects rifampicin resistance.

t.a: Peripheral blood smear for malaria parasites
t.b: Detect low‑density parasitaemia missed by RDT.

b: Persistent high fever >40 °C with lethargy.
Signs of shock: cold extremities, capillary refill >2 s, hypotension.
Severe anemia (Hb <7 g/dL) or thrombocytopenia.
Neurological change: seizures, coma.
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent intervention.

b: Empiric antimalarial (artesunate) if malaria likely and test unavailable.
Broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) for possible bacterial sepsis; avoid aminoglycosides if renal function unknown.
Start antiretroviral therapy only after HIV confirmed; meanwhile, give cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.
If TB suspected, start first‑line anti‑TB regimen (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) after ruling out contraindications.
Fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline for shock; monitor for overload in cardiac disease.
sections.p: Treat the identified cause; if none yet, provide supportive care while investigations continue.

b: Schedule review after 48 h of empiric therapy.
Educate caregivers on malaria prophylaxis and HIV testing.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate daily; adjust therapy as results return. Prevent recurrence with vaccination, vector control, safe water, and early treatment of infections.

b: Sepsis with obvious source – usually identified on exam.
Febrile seizures – brief fever spikes with normal exam.
Autoimmune fever (e.g., Kawasaki) – mucocutaneous changes.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic PUO but have distinct clues.

b: Negative malaria RDT does not exclude low‑parasitaemia; smear needed.
Normal ESR in early TB can be misleading; rely on clinical scoring.
Blood cultures may be sterile after prior antibiotics; consider repeat.

whenToSeekHelp: Altered consciousness, seizures, or persistent fever >40 °C
Signs of shock or severe dehydration
